findings.study_system: emergency-medicine RCTs with nonsignificant primary endpoints

findings.claim: An international forum of health-research funders agreed on ten Guiding Principles that, if adhered to, would reduce research waste and ensure value in research.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The EViR Funders' Forum worked together to develop a set of ten Guiding Principles, that if funders adhered to would reduce research waste and ensure value in research.
findings.evidence: Consensus development by the Ensuring Value in Research (EViR) Funders' Forum.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The EViR Funders' Forum worked together to develop a set of ten Guiding Principles, that if funders adhered to would reduce research waste and ensure value in research.

findings.claim: Overlapping James Lind Alliance priority-setting 'Top 10s' could be combined into collaborative research to increase value and reduce research waste.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Some PSPs share similar priorities, which could be combined, promoted and addressed through collaborative research to increase value and reduce research waste.
findings.evidence: Coproduced synthesis of UK James Lind Alliance Priority Setting Partnership 'Top 10' lists.

findings.claim: Most medRxiv clinical-study preprints were concordant with their peer-reviewed journal versions: 86.4% had concordant sample sizes and 96.2% had concordant final interpretations.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Of the 535 pairs reporting sample sizes in both sources, 462 (86.4%) were concordant; 43 (58.9%) of the 73 pairs with discordant sample sizes had larger samples in the journal publication.
findings.evidence: Cross-sectional study of medRxiv preprint-journal article pairs first posted September 2020.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Overall, 526 pairs (96.2%) had concordant study interpretations, including 82 of the 101 pairs (81.2%) with discordant primary end point results.

findings.claim: A survey of 408 Hungarian researchers found publication pressure did not differ by discipline, but female researchers perceived greater stress than male researchers.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The findings also showed that female researchers perceive greater stress than male researchers.
findings.evidence: Survey using the Revised Publication Pressure Questionnaire across career stages, fields, and genders.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: A total of 408 respondents completed the survey, 46% were female, and 54% were male.

findings.claim: Among 1298 Amsterdam researchers, individual, climate and publication factors together explained 34% of variance in perceived research misbehavior, with research-climate perceptions the largest contributor (22%).
findings.claim_source_sentence: Results showed that individual, climate and publication factors combined explained 34% of variance in perceived frequency of research misbehavior. Individual factors explained 7%, climate factors explained 22% and publication factors 16%.
findings.evidence: Survey integrating three instruments among academic researchers in Amsterdam.
findings.effect_size: climate factors explained 22% of variance; publication factors 16%; total 34%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Results showed that individual, climate and publication factors combined explained 34% of variance in perceived frequency of research misbehavior. Individual factors explained 7%, climate factors explained 22% and publication factors 16%.

findings.claim: Among 244 NSF Graduate Research Fellows, self-reported academic cheating was 16.7% and research misconduct 3.7%, with funding, publication, and tenure pressures cited as the most negative aspects of academia.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The self-reported rate of academic cheating was 16.7% and of research misconduct was 3.7%.
findings.evidence: Anonymous survey of prestigious NSF Graduate Research Fellows in engineering and computer science.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The self-reported rate of academic cheating was 16.7% and of research misconduct was 3.7%.

findings.claim: In an international survey, contract type, career stage, field, adherence to scientific norms and gender significantly predicted engagement in questionable research practices, while between-institution variance was minimal.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Our findings indicate that contract type, career stage, academic field, adherence to scientific norms and gender significantly predict QRP engagement.
findings.evidence: Multi-level modelling of an international survey of researchers on QRP determinants.

findings.claim: Cross-sectional survey of early/mid-career health academics found precarious employment and very high burnout, indicating a poor research-culture/work environment.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Workloads were considerable, with 89.5% of participants working overtime and 54.8% reporting burnout.
findings.evidence: 284 EMCAs at two large Australian universities; half on <1yr contracts, ~90% overtime, ~55% burnout, high rates of bullying/harassment.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Workloads were considerable, with 89.5% of participants working overtime and 54.8% reporting burnout.

findings.claim: Surveys of US postdocs before and during COVID-19 found the pandemic significantly harmed mental health and career confidence across all identities.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We found that respondents' mental health and wellness were significantly impacted by the pandemic irrespective of their gender, race, citizenship, or other identities.
findings.evidence: Compared 2019 and late-2020 postdoc surveys; mental health, career progression, and confidence in achieving career goals all worsened; institutional postdoc offices mitigated impacts.

findings.claim: Among academics, working excessively (workaholism) is most strongly connected to burnout in a network analysis, consistent with publish-or-perish demands harming wellbeing.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In the cross-sample network the strongest connection was burnout -working excessively (.35).
findings.evidence: Psychometric network of 131 academics in Montenegro; workaholism and burnout cluster together; dedication negatively linked to burnout.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In the cross-sample network the strongest connection was burnout -working excessively (.35).
findings.study_system: academics at public/private universities, Montenegro (survey, n=131)

findings.claim: Academic CVs rarely capture rigor/reproducibility/transparency practices, so a new CV template was created to make such practices visible for hiring/promotion/tenure.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Few institutions consider rigor, reproducibility, or transparency practices for hiring, promotion, or tenure decisions.
findings.evidence: Describes a Stanford School of Medicine CV template adding protocol/data/code availability, trial registration, peer-review activity, and ORCID to make reproducibility efforts evaluable.
findings.study_system: academic CV template (Stanford School of Medicine)

findings.claim: Across 7 European countries, researchers consistently perceive reward/merit systems as rewarding speed and quantity over quality and integrity, promoting QRPs.
findings.claim_source_sentence: These systems are widely perceived to reward speed and quantity at the expense of quality and integrity, thereby potentially undermining the robustness of the knowledge produced.
findings.evidence: 36 focus groups, 172 researchers; perceptions consistent across country, discipline, gender, seniority; argues assessment reform must address 'process time' and temporal autonomy.
findings.study_system: researchers across 7 European countries (36 focus groups)

findings.claim: A scoping review found that few research funders currently require narrative CVs, though national granting agencies are early adopters.
findings.claim_source_sentence: First, number of funders currently requiring NCVs remains low overall, although national granting agencies are among the early adopters.
findings.evidence: Grey-literature scoping review of narrative CV templates; low overall adoption, structural commonalities, little guidance on how NCVs are evaluated.
findings.study_system: research funding agencies (scoping review of narrative-CV templates)

findings.claim: Narrative CVs are being piloted as a mechanism to enable qualitative research assessment aligned with DORA/Leiden/CoARA reform.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Narrative CVs have emerged as enabling qualitative assessments and are becoming more widely piloted.
findings.evidence: Workshop report gathering perspectives on narrative-CV implementation, effects on careers, recognition of collaborative work, and equality/diversity/inclusion.

findings.claim: An institution built a scalable, multi-channel research-integrity training programme, reaching over 1200 of 4000+ staff across 15 centres.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Over 1200 of over 4000 of the participants were reached across all 15 KEMRI research centers.
findings.evidence: KEMRI Research Integrity Committee used train-the-trainer, conference symposia, centre-specific training, hybrid delivery, and digital dissemination to institutionalise RCR in an LMIC setting.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Over 1200 of over 4000 of the participants were reached across all 15 KEMRI research centers.

findings.claim: Among Ugandan faculty, prior ethics training was independently associated with lower odds of self-reported research misconduct, but misconduct persisted (31.4% prevalence).
findings.claim_source_sentence: In multivariable analysis, prior ethics training (aOR = 0.27; 95% CI 0.07-0.98; p = 0.046) and the perception that RM is unacceptable (aOR = 0.27; 95% CI 0.07-0.98; p = 0.046) were independently associated with lower odds of self-reported RM.
findings.evidence: Survey of 70 faculty (SMQ-R); 31.4% self-reported FFP; ethics training and viewing RM as unacceptable each lowered odds, but persistence suggests training needs strengthening.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In multivariable analysis, prior ethics training (aOR = 0.27; 95% CI 0.07-0.98; p = 0.046) and the perception that RM is unacceptable (aOR = 0.27; 95% CI 0.07-0.98; p = 0.046) were independently associated with lower odds of self-reported RM.

findings.claim: A randomized educational intervention improved graduate students' authorship knowledge/confidence, with a low-cost online format sufficient (added workshop gave no extra benefit).
findings.claim_source_sentence: The additional workshop did not yield further benefits for students' outcomes, suggesting that institutions can help promote ethical authorship through low-cost, scalable educational resources.
findings.evidence: 185 students underwent online authorship-ethics training plus an authorship-agreement form; half randomized to an extra workshop; online training alone boosted knowledge/confidence.

findings.claim: A manuscript-level meta-research analysis of one journal found reviewer disagreement is common early but usually resolved by editorial adjudication, not by voting.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Reviewer discordance was common in the first round for both published and rejected manuscripts (74.8% and 85.8%).
findings.evidence: Analysis of 12,187 published and 3,819 rejected manuscripts (2021-2025); discordance fell to 29.3% by final round among published papers; ~88% alignment between majority recommendation and outcome, but not absolute.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Reviewer discordance was common in the first round for both published and rejected manuscripts (74.8% and 85.8%).
findings.study_system: editorial peer-review records, one MDPI journal (meta-research)

findings.claim: In Ecuador, reliance on journal-centric metrics predicted lower adoption of open-science practices, while institutional support predicted higher adoption.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Greater reliance on journal-centric metrics was associated with lower odds of adopting open practices (odds ratio ≈ 0.72), while comprehensive institutional support-repositories with deposit mandates, research-data services, and licensing guidance-was associated with higher odds (odds ratio ≈ 1.65).
findings.evidence: Mixed-methods study (policy review, bibliometrics 2013-2023, survey n≈418); high OS familiarity (85%) but only 22% deposited data; assessment incentives shape open practice.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Greater reliance on journal-centric metrics was associated with lower odds of adopting open practices (odds ratio ≈ 0.72), while comprehensive institutional support-repositories with deposit mandates, research-data services, and licensing guidance-was associated with higher odds (odds ratio ≈ 1.65).

findings.claim: A systematic review consolidated the drivers and inhibitors of open research data sharing/use into eleven categories, as a step toward designing effective incentives.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This study systematically analyzed 32 open data studies (published between 2004 and 2019 inclusively) and elicited drivers plus inhibitors for both open research data sharing and use in eleven categories total that are: 'the researcher's background', 'requirements and formal obligations', 'personal drivers and intrinsic motivations', 'facilitating conditions', 'trust', 'expected performance', 'social influence and affiliation', 'effort', 'the researcher's experience and skills', 'legislation and regulation', and 'data characteristics.'
findings.evidence: Thematic synthesis of 32 studies (2004-2019); frames requirements, incentives, and facilitating conditions as key levers; a first step toward effective data-sharing incentives.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: This study systematically analyzed 32 open data studies (published between 2004 and 2019 inclusively) and elicited drivers plus inhibitors for both open research data sharing and use in eleven categories total that are: 'the researcher's background', 'requirements and formal obligations', 'personal drivers and intrinsic motivations', 'facilitating conditions', 'trust', 'expected performance', 'social influence and affiliation', 'effort', 'the researcher's experience and skills', 'legislation and regulation', and 'data characteristics.'

findings.claim: Structured expert elicitation predicted replicability of COVID-19 preprint claims only modestly better than chance, offering a lower-cost complement to running replications.
findings.claim_source_sentence: For experienced individuals, the average accuracy was 0.57 (95% CI: [0.53, 0.61]) after interaction, and they correctly classified 61% of claims; beginners' average accuracy was 0.58 (95% CI: [0.54, 0.62]), correctly classifying 69% of claims.
findings.evidence: 100 preprint claims judged via structured elicitation, 29 new high-powered replications conducted; prediction is a cheaper, faster alternative to replicating everything but accuracy is limited.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: For experienced individuals, the average accuracy was 0.57 (95% CI: [0.53, 0.61]) after interaction, and they correctly classified 61% of claims; beginners' average accuracy was 0.58 (95% CI: [0.54, 0.62]), correctly classifying 69% of claims.

findings.claim: The rising average number of authors per publication, driven partly by perverse incentives and honorary authorship, depreciates the value of authorship credit.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In the long run, INAP depreciates the value of authorship status and may disproportionately impact junior researchers and those who contribute to technical and routine tasks.
findings.evidence: Ethical analysis of the increase in authors per paper (INAP); proposes refining CRediT and adjusting recognition/promotion systems to protect the reward system of science.

findings.claim: Interviews with data-sharing-platform stakeholders found the evaluation system undervalues data contributors, impeding data sharing; contributorship models are proposed.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The evaluation system might impede data sharing because it mainly focuses on first and last authorship and undervalues the contributor's work.
findings.evidence: 17 interviews with EU data-sharing-platform participants; extensive author lists and first/last-author focus disadvantage data generators; favour moving toward contributorship crediting.

findings.claim: Bibliometric analysis shows alphabetical 'middle author' listing is common and grows with team size, complicating credit attribution in team science.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We show that alphabetical ordering of middle authors is frequent in biomedical research, and that the prevalence of this practice is positively correlated with the number of authors in the bylines.
findings.evidence: All Web of Science biomedical articles 1980-2015; for 7+ author papers, more than half of authors are middle authors; middle-author knowledge contribution rose over 35 years.
findings.effect_size: for articles with 7+ authors, more than half are middle authors
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: We also find that, for articles with 7 or more authors, the average proportion of primary, middle and supervisory authors is independent of the team size, more than half of the authors being middle authors.

findings.claim: A scoping review found the evidence base for open-science interventions improving reproducibility is remarkably limited, with few studies measuring the actual outcome.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Of the 105 distinct studies we included, 15 directly measured the effect of an intervention on reproducibility or replicability, while the remainder addressed a proxy outcome that might be expected to increase reproducibility or replicability, such as data sharing, methods transparency or pre-registration.
findings.evidence: 105 studies of reproducibility interventions; only 15 measured reproducibility/replicability directly; 30 non-comparative and 27 cross-sectional, precluding causal inference.
findings.effect_size: 15 of 105 studies measured the effect directly
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Of the 105 distinct studies we included, 15 directly measured the effect of an intervention on reproducibility or replicability, while the remainder addressed a proxy outcome that might be expected to increase reproducibility or replicability, such as data sharing, methods transparency or pre-registration.

findings.claim: The decline of single-author papers reflects not only genuine collaboration but metric-driven 'strategic co-authorship' (honorary/gift authorship, publication cartels).
findings.claim_source_sentence: While this trend is often attributed to increased scientific collaboration and research complexity, substantial evidence suggests that systemic publication pressures and metric-based evaluation systems have created incentives for "strategic co-authorship"-practices including honorary authorship, gift authorship, and publication cartels that violate established authorship criteria.
findings.evidence: Synthesis of bibliometric analyses, prevalence surveys, and academic-culture studies; argues addressing authorship misconduct requires reforming institutional assessment.

findings.claim: A review catalogues how bibliometric metrics are gamed under publish-or-perish incentives, spanning authorship, citation, editorial, and journal-based manipulation and fabrication.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This review examines several gaming practices, including authorship-based, citation-based, editorial-based, and journal-based gaming as well as gaming with outright fabrication.
findings.evidence: Enumerates gift authorship, salami-slicing of credit, massive self-citations, citation farms, H-index gaming, editorial nepotism, impact-factor gaming, and paper mills; proposes metrics that also flag gaming.

findings.claim: A review argues academic pressure and monetary publication incentives are the main drivers of the mass-produced 'fake paper' (paper-mill) flood.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The main drivers of the fake paper flood are the pressure in academic systems and (monetary) incentives to publish in respected scientific journals and sometimes the personal desire for increased 'prestige.'
findings.evidence: Review of paper mills selling fabricated manuscripts at scale; links the problem directly to academic incentive systems; outlines detection information sources.

findings.claim: Journal-prestige (impact-factor) evaluation overlooks most influential work, because far more papers are as well-cited as those in high-IF journals than are published there.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We also find that approximately half of researchers never publish in a venue with an impact factor above 15, which, under journal-level evaluation regimes, may exclude them from consideration for opportunities.
findings.evidence: Quantifies that journal hierarchies may recognize as little as 10-20% of influential work; effect holds across gender, race, and career stage; supports article-level over journal-level metrics.
findings.effect_size: journal-level metrics may recognize as little as 10%-20% of influential work
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Many of these researchers publish equally influential work; however, raising the possibility that the traditionally chosen journal-level measures that are routinely considered under decision-making norms, policy, or law, may recognize as little as 10%-20% of this influential work.

findings.claim: Analysis of retracted AI-related papers shows retractions surged in 2023 and are heavily concentrated in a few countries, driven by peer-review and data problems.
findings.claim_source_sentence: A total of 764 retracted AI-related papers were examined, with the most retractions occurring in 2023 (n = 667).
findings.evidence: 764 retracted AI papers in PubMed; China n=551, India n=40, Bangladesh n=23; leading reasons peer-review issues (n=716) and data concerns (n=714); median time to retraction 510 days.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: A total of 764 retracted AI-related papers were examined, with the most retractions occurring in 2023 (n = 667).

findings.claim: A forensic red-flagging method estimated that about 5.8% of the biomedical literature consists of fabricated 'fake' papers, roughly 107,800 articles per year.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Applying Bayes' rule resulted in an estimate of 5.8% actual fakes in the biomedical literature.
findings.evidence: Multifactorial red-flagging rule (94% sensitivity, 11.5% false-alarm rate); red-flagged fraction rose to ~16.3% in 2023; Bayesian estimate ~5.8% true fakes (~107,800/yr).
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The multifactorial tallying rule was the best red-flagging method, with a 94% sensitivity and only a 11.5% false-alarm rate.

findings.claim: A machine-learning model trained on retracted paper-mill papers flagged nearly 10% of 2.6 million cancer research papers as potentially fraudulent.
findings.claim_source_sentence: When applied to the cancer research literature, it flagged 261 245 of 2 647 471 papers (9.87%, 95% confidence interval 9.83 to 9.90)
findings.evidence: ML classifier (accuracy 0.91) trained on paper-mill retractions; flagged 9.87% of 2.6M cancer papers (1999-2024); >170,000 Chinese-affiliated papers (36% of Chinese cancer articles) flagged.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: When applied to the cancer research literature, it flagged 261 245 of 2 647 471 papers (9.87%, 95% confidence interval 9.83 to 9.90)

findings.claim: In a survey of 452 professors across US and Indian universities, awareness of the reproducibility crisis was high (>91.5% USA, 83.8% India), yet among those who attempted to replicate others' work only 14.58% of Indian and 33.96% of US researchers obtained affirmative (successful) results.
findings.claim_source_sentence: 14.58% of Indian researchers who reported trying to replicate others’ research obtained affirmative results with the remaining majority reporting unsuccessful or only partially successful results.
findings.evidence: Cross-national survey of academic faculty attitudes toward and experiences with reproducibility/replicability.
findings.effect_size: 14.58% (India) vs 33.96% (USA) of replication attempts obtained affirmative results
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In comparison, 33.96% of respondents in the USA who engaged in replication of others’ work reported affirmative results.
findings.study_system: Survey of 452 professors in the USA (n=261) and India (n=191)

findings.claim: A pre-post evaluation of an open-science/responsible-research-practices course found engagement with open-science tooling rose sharply (OSF accounts 7 to 78) but concrete outputs (preregistrations, protocols, shared datasets, preprints) remained absent both before and after.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The number of OSF accounts increased from 7 to 78 after the end of the course.
findings.evidence: Pre-post intervention study measuring adoption of open-science practices among course participants.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The number of OSF accounts increased from 7 to 78 after the end of the course.
findings.study_system: Pre-post study of an open-science/responsible-research-practices training course, n=80 participants

findings.claim: A meta-research review of data-transparency documents the gap between pledged and actual data sharing: among 1,792 manuscripts whose data-availability statements explicitly promised sharing, 93% of authors did not respond or declined, and only 6.8% ultimately supplied their datasets.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Among the 1,792 manuscripts whose DAS explicitly pledged data sharing, 1,669 authors (93%) either did not respond or declined to provide their data.
findings.evidence: Review synthesizing empirical evidence on the disconnect between data-availability statements and actual data provision.
findings.effect_size: 93% (1,669/1,792) did not provide data; only 123 (6.8%) supplied datasets
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Consequently, only 123 authors (6.8%) ultimately supplied the requested datasets
findings.study_system: Meta-research review of data-availability statements in biomedical papers (reports a cohort of 1,792 manuscripts pledging data sharing)

findings.claim: An open-access citation-advantage analysis of 43,275 medical-education articles found PMCID-indexed (OA) articles averaged 16.22 versus 13.19 citations for non-OA (~23% more) and higher Relative Citation Ratios (1.17 vs 0.87), all differences p<.001.
findings.claim_source_sentence: PMCID-indexed articles achieved an (untrimmed) average of 16.22 versus 13.19 citations in the non-OA segment
findings.evidence: Scientometric comparison of citation impact between open-access and non-open-access medical-education publications.
findings.effect_size: 16.22 vs 13.19 mean citations (OA vs non-OA); RCR 1.17 vs 0.87; ~23% citation advantage
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The RCR averaged 1.17 for OA versus 0.87 for non-OA articles (untrimmed)
findings.study_system: Scientometric analysis of 43,275 medical-education research articles (OA vs non-OA)

findings.claim: A regression analysis of 97,806 orthopaedic articles found open-access status independently predicted higher annual citation rates (coefficient 0.175, 95% CI 0.071-0.279, p=0.001), alongside number of authors (coefficient 0.108 per author).
findings.claim_source_sentence: The coefficient for OA status was 0.175 (95% CI 0.071 to 0.279, p = 0.001)
findings.evidence: Scientometric regression modelling drivers of citation performance in orthopaedic research.
findings.effect_size: OA coefficient 0.175 (95% CI 0.071-0.279, p=0.001) additional citations/year
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The coefficient for OA status was 0.175 (95% CI 0.071 to 0.279, p = 0.001)
findings.study_system: Scientometric regression analysis of 97,806 orthopaedic articles

findings.claim: An assessment of selective-reporting-bias handling in 49 Campbell systematic reviews found most (40/49) conducted some structured reporting-bias assessment but only 12 (24%) fully documented their outcome/analysis reporting-bias evaluations.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Only 12 reviews provided full documentation for their ORB/ARB assessments.
findings.evidence: Systematic review auditing how Campbell reviews assess and document selective reporting bias in included studies.
findings.effect_size: 12 of 49 reviews (24%) fully documented; 40 of 49 conducted some assessment
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Most (40 of 49) reviews conducted some structured assessment of reporting biases, but many did not report results of these assessments.
findings.study_system: Systematic review of 49 Campbell Collaboration systematic reviews

findings.claim: A transparency/reproducibility audit of 255 animal-model opioid-addiction studies found near-total absence of open-science practices: 0% preregistered, raw data available for only 3.1%, 0% shared analytical code, and 94.5% lacked sample-size justification.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The raw data were available and accessible for only 3.1% of articles.
findings.evidence: Meta-research assessment of transparency and reproducibility indicators across animal-model opioid-addiction publications.
findings.effect_size: 3.1% data available; 0% preregistered; 0% shared code; 94.5% no sample-size justification
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: No (0%) papers stated that any of their studies were preregistered or were in a registered report format.
findings.study_system: Meta-research audit of 255 articles using animal models of opioid addiction

findings.claim: A case study of an individual-participant-data meta-analysis found that even after contacting trialists, only 60.8% (48/79) responded and only 20.8% of responders shared their IPD, illustrating how data-sharing norms fail at the point of request.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Trialists from 48 of 79 trials (60.8%) responded to the IPD-MA invitation (Table 3), while trialists from the remaining 31 trials (39.2%) did not respond.
findings.evidence: Empirical case study documenting response and data-provision rates when contacting trialists for IPD.

findings.study_system: Case study of an IPD meta-analysis contacting trialists from 79 trials

findings.claim: A scoping review of the academic impact of Open Science found the citation advantage is real but inconsistent: 47.8% of reviewed studies found an open-access citation advantage (27.6% found none, 23.9% only in subsets), and openly shared data was associated with roughly 9% more citations.
findings.claim_source_sentence: 47.8% of reviewed studies found an OACA, with the remaining studies finding no OACA (27.6%) or only in subsets (23.9%)
findings.evidence: Scoping review synthesizing evidence on citation and attention advantages of open-science practices.
findings.effect_size: 47.8% of studies found an open-access citation advantage; open data associated with ~9% more citations
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: publications that share data openly receive 9% more citations than publications that did not share data openly
findings.study_system: Scoping review of studies measuring the academic impact (citations/attention) of open-science practices

findings.claim: A large multi-study replication project in sports and exercise science found weak replicability: only 28% of replications were deemed successful (significance plus compatible effect size), 56% had the same significance-testing outcome as the original, and 36% had compatible effect-size estimates.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Overall, 28% of the replications were deemed successful as they achieved statistical significance and compatible effect size estimates
findings.evidence: Reflections paper reporting the outcomes of a large coordinated replication project.
findings.effect_size: 28% successful; 56% same NHST outcome; 36% compatible effect sizes
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: our overall findings were that 56% had the same null hypothesis significance testing outcomes as the original studies
findings.study_system: Large replication project in sports and exercise science

findings.claim: A bibliometric analysis of the biomedical research-waste literature identified 876 publications cited 39,768 times (average 45.4 citations/article), led by the United States (136 articles), with The Lancet the top venue (48 publications, 5.49% of the total).
findings.claim_source_sentence: the 876 publications collected were cited a cumulative total of 39 768 times, yielding an average citation frequency of 45.4 citations per article.
findings.evidence: Bibliometric mapping of the research-waste literature's growth, geography, and venues.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: the 876 publications collected were cited a cumulative total of 39 768 times, yielding an average citation frequency of 45.4 citations per article.
findings.study_system: Bibliometric analysis of 876 biomedical research-waste publications

findings.claim: An exploratory survey of 83 behavioral-addictions researchers found open-science practices are becoming normative in this field: preregistration (76%) and data sharing (65%) were the most commonly used, with mostly positive attitudes.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The most commonly used practices were preregistration (76%) and data sharing (65%).
findings.evidence: Survey of self-reported open-science practice adoption among researchers in one subfield.
findings.effect_size: preregistration used by 76%; data sharing by 65%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The most commonly used practices were preregistration (76%) and data sharing (65%).

findings.claim: An audit of authorship guidance on 145 R1 US university websites found weak institutional support for responsible authorship: only 41% (59/145) instructed prospective authors to meet and discuss authorship expectations, and only 42% (61/145) explicitly linked credit with accountability.
findings.claim_source_sentence: only 59 out of 145 (41%) instructed prospective authors to meet to discuss authorship expectations
findings.evidence: Content analysis of institutional authorship guidelines to assess anchoring in transparency, credit, and accountability principles.
findings.effect_size: 59/145 (41%) instruct authorship discussion; 61/145 (42%) link credit with accountability

findings.study_system: Content analysis of authorship guidelines from 145 R1 US university websites

findings.claim: An analysis of an early study registry in parapsychology (the KPU Study Registry, operating since 2012) found preregistered studies reported far fewer significant results than non-preregistered ones (16% vs 46.6%), mirroring the effect later seen in mainstream psychology's registered reports.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In line with previous work within mainstream psychology, the preregistered studies contained fewer significant results (16%) than non-preregistered experiments (46.6%).
findings.evidence: Comparison of positive-result rates between preregistered and non-preregistered studies in the same field/period.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In line with previous work within mainstream psychology, the preregistered studies contained fewer significant results (16%) than non-preregistered experiments (46.6%).
findings.study_system: Preregistered (KPU Study Registry) vs non-preregistered parapsychology studies, 2012 onward

findings.claim: The Stockholm Declaration (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences) frames paper mills and metric-gaming as an existential threat to science and calls for realigning incentives to reward quality over quantity in a distorted reputation economy.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Adjust incentive systems to merit quality, not quantity, in a reputation economy where the gaming of publication numbers and citation metrics distorts the perception of academic excellence.
findings.evidence: Consensus action plan drafted by a scientific academy conference on publishing reform.
findings.study_system: Stockholm Declaration action plan on science-publishing reform

findings.claim: A systems framework for research trustworthiness argues that trust should rest on measurable indicators of whether research is accountable, evaluable, well-formulated, evaluated, bias-controlled, error-reducing, and warranted by evidence, rather than on any single dimension such as integrity, transparency, or peer review.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We offer a systems approach that focuses on whether the research is accountable, evaluable, well-formulated, has been evaluated, controls for bias, reduces error, and whether the claims are warranted by the evidence.
findings.evidence: Conceptual metascience framework tying trustworthiness to measurable indicators.
findings.study_system: Conceptual framework for trustworthiness indicators of research findings

findings.claim: A multi-author 'scientists' warning' argues that unnecessary bureaucratic burden is a systemic drain on research productivity, diverting scientists from creative work and eroding motivation, framing it as a global impediment requiring a governance charter.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Unnecessary bureaucratic measures limit productivity, waste vital resources and drain workforces of engagement, enthusiasm, motivation, commitment and cohesion.
findings.evidence: Editorial synthesizing the effects of administrative burden on research and proposing a corrective framework.
findings.study_system: Editorial/scientists' warning on bureaucratic burden in research

findings.claim: A proposed 'peer replication' model would add a higher publication tier for works whose results are independently reproduced before publication, positioning reproducibility (rather than peer opinion) as the gatekeeping standard.
findings.claim_source_sentence: To address the replication crisis and instill confidence in the scientific literature, we introduce a new framework for evaluating scientific manuscripts.
findings.evidence: Proposal for restructuring manuscript evaluation around independent replication.
findings.study_system: Proposed 'peer replication' framework for manuscript evaluation

findings.claim: An analysis of stem-cell science hyperbole argues that exaggerated claims are not primarily individual failings but are propagated by contemporary incentive structures and organizational cultures that reward attention over accuracy.
findings.claim_source_sentence: While such norms as truthfulness, accuracy, and accountability might seem self-evident, contemporary incentive structures and organizational cultures play an important role in promoting hyperbolic representations and other inaccurate representations of scientific research.
findings.evidence: Analysis linking reward structures to overclaiming in a competitive research field.
findings.study_system: Analysis of incentive/cultural drivers of stem-cell science hyperbole

findings.claim: A historical review of two crises in social psychology (1960s-70s and 2010-present) concludes that misaligned incentives contributed to both and that a more coordinated approach is needed to prevent a future third crisis.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Finally, I reflect on the extent that the incentives contributed to these crises and argue that a more coordinated approach to scientific research is needed to prevent these concerns from resurfacing in a future third crisis.
findings.evidence: Comparative historical analysis of recurring methodological/incentive crises in a discipline.
findings.study_system: Historical review of two replication/reform crises in social psychology

findings.claim: A 'generosity as scientific method' framework proposes credit-sharing, openness, and stewardship as structured practices that improve rigor and reproducibility while directly countering vanity metrics and short-term incentives in research assessment.
findings.claim_source_sentence: I outline practical principles for embedding generosity into research design, governance, and evaluation and discuss how these principles can counter vanity metrics and short-term incentives.
findings.evidence: Conceptual viewpoint positioning collaborative norms against competition-driven evaluation.
findings.study_system: Conceptual framework: generosity as counter to competition-driven metrics

findings.claim: An analysis of the NIH 2025 Public Access Policy warns that eliminating embargoes expands who can read science but, without curbing article processing charges and market concentration, risks shifting the barrier from readers to authors who cannot afford to publish.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Yet without addressing article processing charges and market concentration, the policy risks creating new barriers to who can afford to perform and publish their science.
findings.evidence: Policy analysis of open-access mandate economics and equity effects.
findings.study_system: Policy analysis of the NIH 2025 Public Access Policy and APC economics

findings.claim: An observational study of Peru's national researcher registry (RENACYT; 9,651 researchers, 92,284 publications, 2019-2024) found productivity-based tiers capture output and journal-quality gradients but poorly differentiate scientific leadership and integrity, with retractions positively associated with productivity.
findings.claim_source_sentence: RENACYT captures gradients in productivity and quality but insufficiently differentiates leadership and integrity.
findings.evidence: National research-evaluation system analysed across productivity, journal impact, corresponding authorship, and retractions.
findings.effect_size: 9,651 researchers; 92,284 publications; retractions positively associated with productivity
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: A total of 92,284 publications were identified.
findings.study_system: Observational study of Peru's RENACYT registry (9,651 researchers, 2019-2024)

findings.claim: A meta-research cataloguing project argues that dominant 'Open Science' framings privilege STEM/positivist methods, and that openness in the arts, humanities and social sciences is diverse, situated, context-dependent, and resistant to the quantification and binary measurement used in open-science monitoring.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Presenting a typology of forms of openness in AHSS that is consistent with the epistemic logics of these disciplines, we conclude that openness in AHSS is highly situated and context-dependent, as well as resisting quantification and binary measurement.
findings.evidence: Literature review, desk research, and conceptual mapping producing a typology of open-research practices across disciplines.
findings.study_system: Meta-research cataloguing open-research practices in arts, humanities and social sciences (MORPHSS project)

findings.claim: A review of Global South scholarly-communication initiatives (Latin America, Africa, Asia) argues that free-to-read, free-to-publish, multilingual, publicly funded and scholarly-led non-profit models offer a fairer blueprint than APC-based commercial open access.
findings.claim_source_sentence: These initiatives also promote multilingualism, public funding, and non-profit, scholarly-led governance structures.
findings.evidence: Point-of-view review of community-driven, non-commercial publishing models.
findings.study_system: Review of Global South scholarly-publishing initiatives (Latin America, Africa, Asia)

establishing.thesis: The persistence of the data-welfare debt is not a technical accident but a predictable output of the incentive system: evaluation rewards publication counts and journal impact while pricing data sharing at near-zero, questionable research practices are common, and declared openness vastly exceeds actual openness. Reform proposals exist but the evidence that they change behaviour - rather than metrics - is thin.
establishing.synthesis: If incentives explain why voluntary stewardship fails, sec-governance asks what enforced standards, mandates and reporting guidelines can actually achieve, and where they fall short.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: We then illustrate how one can test for p-hacking when performing a meta-analysis and show that, while p-hacking is probably common, its effect seems to be weak relative to the real effect sizes being measured.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Magnitude of distortion: the p-hacking text-mining study concludes analytic flexibility is common but only weakly distorts meta-analytic consensus, whereas the theoretical framework concludes bias/flexibility make most published findings outright false.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: This finding suggests that some questionable practices may constitute the prevailing research norm.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: The prevalence estimates, however, do not suggest outright systematic use of specific QRPs.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Interpretation of QRP prevalence: the incentivised psychology survey frames QRPs as the prevailing norm, while the cross-national study argues widespread one-time involvement does not amount to systematic/normative use once frequency is measured.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: There is some evidence from both simulations and empirical studies supporting the likely effectiveness of these measures, but their broad adoption by researchers, institutions, funders and journals will require iterative evaluation and improvement.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: We additionally show that replication slows but does not stop the process of methodological deterioration.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Reform optimism: the manifesto expects methods/reporting/incentive measures to improve reliability, whereas the natural-selection model argues that as long as publication drives careers, incentives keep selecting bad methods and researcher-level fixes (even replication) are insufficient without institutional change.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: We find that the publication of potentially non-replicable studies minimizes cost and maximizes efficiency of knowledge gain for the scientific community under a variety of assumptions.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Thus, negative studies were published at scarcely more than 10% the rate of positive studies.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether publishing potentially non-replicable / positive-only results is efficient (Lewandowsky & Oberauer model) or corrupts the record by canonizing false facts through publication bias (Nissen et al. model).

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Empirical evidence has also found that Registered Reports are perceived to be higher in research quality than regular articles, as well as equivalent in creativity and importance, while also allowing to report more negative results, which may provide further incentives for researchers to adopt this format.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Median power to detect small, medium, and large effects was 0.12, 0.44, and 0.73, reflecting no improvement through the past half-century.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Optimism about reform: the credibility-revolution review argues open-science reforms have produced substantive improvement, whereas the power meta-analysis finds no improvement in statistical power over half a century.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Across the four comparison journals, for the half years prior to 2014, an average of 3.3% of articles reported open data (range = 1.6% to 4.9%), and after January 1, 2014, the average was 2.1% (range = 1.8% to 2.3%).
conflicts.paper_b_claim: In most studies (56%), the archived datasets were incomplete, either because of missing data or insufficient metadata, resulting in a completeness score of 3 or less (Figs 1 and 2A).
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether transparency interventions deliver genuinely usable open data: badges increased data that was actually available/usable, whereas audits of mandated archives found most datasets incomplete or unusable.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: of 334 articles declaring that they would share data, only 2 IPD sets (0.6%; 95% CI, 0.0%-1.5%) were actually deidentified and publicly available on the journal website.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: When badges were earned, reportedly available data were more likely to be actually available, correct, usable, and complete than when badges were not earned.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether a policy requirement translates into actually available data: a blanket journal data-sharing mandate (ICMJE) produced near-zero actual public data (0.6%), whereas a voluntary badge-plus-verification incentive increased data that was actually available and usable.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: This article provides an overview of recent evidence suggesting that this narrative is mistaken, and argues that a narrative of epochal changes and empowerment of scientists would be more accurate, inspiring, and compelling.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether science faces a genuine reproducibility/false-findings crisis: Ioannidis' framework concludes most published findings are likely false, whereas Fanelli argues the crisis narrative is empirically mistaken and overstated, which bears directly on how urgently incentive/reform interventions are justified.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The probability of papers to support the tested hypothesis increased significantly with the per capita academic productivity of the state of the corresponding author (b = 1.383±0.682, Wald test = 4.108, df = 1, p = 0.043, Odds-Ratio (95%CI) = 3.988(1.047–15.193),).
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Authors publishing at high rates and receiving many citations were, overall, not at greater risk of bias.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether productivity pressure inflates bias: Fanelli's US-states analysis found higher academic productivity predicted more hypothesis-confirming papers, whereas the later cross-disciplinary meta-assessment (Fanelli, Costas & Ioannidis) found high-output, highly cited authors were overall not at greater risk of bias.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Although often derided, quantitative metrics could help improve research practices if they are rigorous, field-adjusted, and centralized.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Highlights the incompatibility between universities' alignment with socially responsible practices and continued engagement with socially irresponsible ranking practices.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether quantitative/ranking metrics can be reformed into a force that improves research (pro-metrics) or are inherently socially irresponsible instruments that should be resisted (anti-ranking).

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Meta-analysis yielded a pooled weighted estimate of 1.97% (95%CI: 0.86–4.45), with significant heterogeneity (Cochran's Q = 61.7777, df = 6, P<0.0001).
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Applying Bayes' rule resulted in an estimate of 5.8% actual fakes in the biomedical literature.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Prevalence of data fabrication: survey self-reports pool to ~2% of scientists admitting fabrication, whereas forensic red-flagging/detection of the biomedical literature estimates ~5.8% of papers are actual fakes (and ML screening flags ~9.87% of cancer papers), implying self-report substantially underestimates fabrication relative to detection-based methods.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: 47.8% of reviewed studies found an OACA, with the remaining studies finding no OACA (27.6%) or only in subsets (23.9%)
conflicts.paper_b_claim: PMCID-indexed articles achieved an (untrimmed) average of 16.22 versus 13.19 citations in the non-OA segment
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether open access confers a citation advantage: the scoping review finds it inconsistent (fewer than half of studies detect an advantage, over a quarter find none), whereas the single-field empirical study reports a clear ~23% advantage at p<.001. The disagreement is on the robustness and generality of the open-access citation advantage across fields and designs.
